blocks.text: There remains the pheasant, which in former times seems to have been the very summit of delicacies. Thus, according to Athenaeus, book 14, Ptolemy Physcon, although he kept pheasants in great numbers in Egypt, οὐδὲ φασιανικοῦ ὄρνιθός ποτε γεύσασθαι ὡμολόγησεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ τι κειμήλιον ἀνακείμενον εἶχε τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας [oude phasianikou ornithos pote geusasthai hōmologēsen, all᾽ hōsper ti keimēlion anakeimenon eiche tous de tous ornithas], declared that he had never tasted a pheasant, but kept these birds as a stored-up treasure. So in Capitolinus Pertinax never ate a pheasant (fasianus, for there it is written with f) at a private banquet, nor sent one to anyone. In Lampridius, Alexander Severus served pheasant at his table only on the Kalends of January, at the Hilaria of the Mother of the Gods, at the Apollinarian games, at the feast of Jupiter, at the Saturnalia, and on festival days of that kind. In Vopiscus, the emperor Tacitus served the pheasant bird only on his own birthday and those of his family, and on the most festive days. And, as Ammianus attests in book 2, Julian forbade a pheasant to be demanded or brought in at the banquet of the Caesar. Evidently rarity added value to a bird that was excellent in itself. Petronius in the Satyricon:
The bird sought from Phasian Colchis, And African fowl please the palate, Because they are not easy to get. — — —

The bird sought from Phasian Colchis, that is, the pheasant, fetched from the Phasis, a river of Colchis. For it was brought from there, as the name itself shows. Agatharchides on the Phasis, in Athenaeus, book 9: Πλῆθος δὲ ὀρνίθων τῶν καλουμένων φασιανῶν φοιτᾷ τροφῆς χάριν πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν στομάτων [Plēthos de ornithōn tōn kaloumenōn phasianōn phoita trophēs charin pros tas embolas tōn stomatōn]; A great multitude of the birds they call pheasants resorts to the mouths of the river for the sake of food. Petronius likewise elsewhere:
— — — — Now the Phasis' wave Is bereft of its birds. — — — —
I was first carried over in the Argive keel: Before that nothing was known to me but the Phasis.
Statius in The Parrot of Melior, book 2 of the Silvae:

Whom neither the Junonian bird with jewelled tail Could surpass in beauty, nor the bird of the icy Phasis. [II, 655] Clement in the Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 1: Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται ἀπὸ Φάσιδος [Orneis epi toutois synōnountai apo Phasidos]; Besides, they buy up birds from the Phasis. Apollonius in Philostratus, book 8, ch. 3: Οὐ κρίνω τοὺς τρυφῶντας ὑπὲρ τοῦ φοινικέου ὄρνιθος, οὐδ' ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἐκ Φάσιδος, ἢ Παιόνων [Ou krinō tous tryphōntas hyper tou phoinikeou ornithos, oud' hyper tou ek Phasidos, ē Paionōn]; I do not bring to judgement those given to luxury on account of the crimson bird (the flamingo), nor on account of the bird from the Phasis or from the Paeonians, that is, the pheasant or the crane. Jordanes, On the Affairs of the Goths, ch. 21: To the river Phasis, from which the Phasian birds have come forth that abound throughout the whole world at the banquets of the powerful. Eustathius on Dionysius: Οἱ φασιανοὶ δὲ τὸ ὄρνεον ἐκεῖθεν παρονομασθῆναι δοκοῦσιν ὡς αὐτόθι πλεονάσαντες [Hoi phasianoi de to orneon ekeithen paronomasthēnai dokousin hōs autothi pleonasantes]; The pheasants, a species of bird, seem to have had their [col. 96] name from there, as having abounded in that place. These things, however commonplace, nevertheless escaped the Talmudists and the Chaldee paraphrasts. For they would not have taken for pheasants the birds that the south wind had brought into the camp of the Israelites, had they known that pheasants are brought from the north. I admit, indeed, that pheasants are not sought from Colchis alone. For to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, ἐκ Μηδείας μετεπέμποντο [ek Mēdeias metepempontō], they were fetched from Media, as Athenaeus testifies in the place cited above. And in the province of Ergimul, Paulus Venetus, book 1, ch. 62, describes very large pheasants, having tails ten or eight palms long. But like Colchis and Media, Ergimul too faces the north, for it is part of Tartary. It seems to be the جرمق [jrmq] giormok of the Arabs, because the name is close and in both places there is musk. See the Nubian Geographer, section 9, Clim. 3. The pheasant is called by another name τατύρας [tatyras] tatyras. So testify Hesychius, and Athenaeus in book 9, following Pamphilus of Alexandria in his Glossary and Epaenetus in his Opsartyticus. I have thought this worth noting because the Persian name of the pheasant, تذرو [tadhrū] tazeru, and the Arabic تدرج [tadruj] tadrug, allude to it.
